title: The Lord's Prayer: A Bible Study Line by Line
subtitle: A five-session study on the Lord's Prayer, line by line, past the recitation and into the words.
summary:
This study is for anyone who has said the Lord's Prayer a thousand times and stopped hearing it, for the small group that wants to learn to pray and doesn't know where to begin, and for the skeptic who suspects the whole thing is a formula recited on autopilot. It moves slowly through five sessions, one for each movement of the prayer Jesus taught when his disciples asked him how to pray. We start with the address, "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name," and refuse to let either the closeness or the awe swallow the other. We take the two petitions that pray against our own preferences, "your kingdom come, your will be done," and ask what it costs to mean them. We find dependence and enough in the request for daily bread. We face the small, hard word as in "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." And we end where the prayer ends, with "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil," and the kingdom and the power and the glory that were never ours. A volunteer can lead it with little preparation: every question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends by praying the line it studied.

This isn't a study that stands above prayer and hands out technique. Many of us have prayed with our mouths while our minds wandered to the calendar, said "Our Father" for years before the word meant anything, and asked God to forgive us in the same breath we refused to forgive someone else. I have. And the one thing this study won't do is turn the Lord's Prayer into a method for getting what we want from God. Most of the prayer is about God's name, kingdom and will before it ever mentions our bread, and the whole of it is built to make us smaller and God larger, which is the opposite of what we usually come to prayer hoping to arrange.
audience: New believers, seasoned Christians, seekers, and small groups learning to pray

sessions.title: Our Father in Heaven, Hallowed Be Your Name
sessions.aim: To hear the first line of the prayer as both astonishingly close and deeply holy, to refuse the sentiment that makes God only a friend and the fear that makes him only a judge, and to sit with what it means that Jesus taught us to begin by calling God Father.
sessions.summary:
Plenty of people can recite the Lord's Prayer long before they believe a word of it, and for some, when belief finally comes, the word that stops them is the first one. Father. For anyone whose own father was absent or harsh, that word can carry nothing, or carry an ache they've learned to walk around. So the question for tonight isn't whether the prayer is familiar. It's whether we've ever really heard its opening line.

Jesus did something in that line that should have stopped the room. In Gethsemane he prayed "Abba, Father" (Mark 14:36), and in this prayer he hands his disciples the right to call God Father too. Joachim Jeremias argued that no Jewish prayer before Jesus addressed God with that family word; James Barr later showed that Abba doesn't simply mean "Daddy." The correction is fair, and the wonder survives it. The Son gave away his own closeness to the Father.

But the line doesn't stop at Father. It says "Father in heaven" and "hallowed be your name" (Matthew 6:9). Our age has rightly recovered God's nearness and quietly lost his holiness, until God becomes a comfort that exists to affirm us. The prayer won't let us choose. It holds the Father we may come close to and the Holy One whose name the seraphim can't look at, and it gives us both in one breath.

keyScripture.why: "Pray then like this: 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name'" (Matthew 6:9). In one breath Jesus gives us the closeness of a Father and the holiness of a name set apart, so the God we're invited to approach as family is never reduced to a comfortable equal.

discussion.q: Most of us have said this prayer hundreds of times. Which word in it do you say without hearing, and what would it take to hear it?
discussion.behind: Open on the gap between reciting and praying. You're not shaming anyone for knowing the words well; you're noticing that the most repeated prayer in the world is often the least heard. Let people be candid about their own autopilot, and resist offering a concentration technique. Go first if the room is slow.

discussion.q: Read Mark 14:36 and Romans 8:15. Jesus prays "Abba, Father" in the garden, and Paul says the Spirit puts the same cry in our mouths. What does it mean to be handed the word Jesus used, and what makes it hard to receive?
discussion.behind: For some the difficulty is unbelief. For others it's a wounded relationship with their own father that has spoiled the word. Make room for both without diagnosing anyone. The word Father isn't neutral in a room full of real histories, and receiving the gift can cost something.

discussion.q: The line goes on: "in heaven, hallowed be your name." Where have you let God become only tender and familiar, and what's lost when the awe goes out of him?
discussion.behind: Hold the other half. A God who is only comfortable is finally too small to save. Help the room feel that the awe isn't the enemy of closeness but its depth. Don't swing people from sentiment into fear; keep both in view.

discussion.q: Our age recovered the nearness of God after a long stretch of picturing him as distant. What was right about that recovery, and where does it turn into a God made in our own image?
discussion.behind: Grant the recovery fully first. A God held so far off that nobody could love him was a real distortion, and a God who runs to meet the prodigal heals that. Then name where it goes wrong: a God shrunk to someone who only ever agrees with us. Fair account first, then the turn.

discussion.q: Many of us pray the word Father for years before we can feel that it means anything. Is praying words your heart hasn't caught up to hypocrisy, or can it be faith?
discussion.behind: Move toward relief. The gap between the words and the heart isn't always hypocrisy. Sometimes it's faith reaching past the feeling, the way a wound heals before it feels healed. Let people stop condemning themselves for wandering minds and start praying from inside the gap. Answer it yourself first, briefly.

objections.objection: Calling God Father is wish fulfillment, a human parent projected onto the sky, just what Freud said religion was. People who never grew up invent a cosmic dad to feel safe.
objections.response: Freud was pointing at something real, so take it seriously. People do project. Plenty of us picture God in the shape of our own father, warm or cold or gone, and the church has often let that picture stand unexamined. Grant that. But the projection theory has a hard time with what Jesus actually reveals, because the Father he names is repeatedly not the father we'd have invented. His name is holy, his will crosses ours, and his kingdom overturns the one we'd build. A projection flatters us; this Father convicts us. And Jesus reverses the order the objection assumes. He doesn't say God is a bit like a human father. He treats the Father in heaven as the original and every human father as the copy: "If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!" (Matthew 7:11). On that reading, the ache of the fatherless isn't evidence that Father is a fiction. It's evidence of what they were made for and didn't receive. We didn't invent the Father. We were made by him, and we've been missing him.

objections.objection: The Lord's Prayer is a religious formula, recited by rote in every church and mouthed by millions who aren't really praying. What's the point of memorized words?
objections.response: That's often true, and Jesus warned about it himself: "And when you pray, do not heap up empty phrases as the Gentiles do, for they think that they will be heard for their many words" (Matthew 6:7). Reciting with a wandering mind is a real danger, and this study won't pretend otherwise. But look at the assumption underneath, that words we make up are sincere and words we've memorized are dead. That doesn't hold up against the way people actually love. Wedding vows are memorized. A grieving family reaches for old words learned by heart, because in that hour they can't compose their own. When the disciples asked to be taught, Jesus didn't tell them to invent something. He said, "Pray then like this" (Matthew 6:9), and gave them words to grow into, the way a young plant is tied to a trellis until it can stand. Set words aren't the enemy of sincerity. They train it, and they wait for the heart to catch up.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: When you say the word Father to God, whose face do you actually see, and what would change if you saw the Father Jesus was pointing to instead of the one you were given?
sessions.practice: This week, pray only the first line: "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name." Go no further. Say it slowly once each morning and stay with it long enough to feel both halves, the nearness of Father and the holiness of hallowed. When your mind wanders, don't scold it; just come back to the line. Write down what rises in you at the word Father, and whether it's the God Jesus revealed you're picturing or someone else wearing his name.
sessions.closingPrayer: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name. We've said these words so long we stopped hearing them, and some of us have said Father with an ache we didn't know where to put. Teach us that you are the Father every human father was meant to point toward, the one we were made for and missed. And teach us in the same breath that your name is holy, that you aren't a comfort we made up but the God the seraphim can't look upon. Draw us close enough to call you Abba, and keep us low enough to hallow your name, and don't let us trade one for the other. Amen.
reflection: Which word of this prayer have I been saying without hearing, and what would it take to hear it?
Is the God I picture when I pray the Father Jesus revealed, or someone built out of my own history?
Have I let God become so familiar that the awe went out of him, or so distant that I forgot I'm invited to call him Father?
sessions.teaching:
Plenty of people can recite the Lord's Prayer before they believe a word of it. They have it by heart the way you keep a childhood phone number, lodged in memory and meaning nothing until the day it suddenly means a great deal. And for some, when belief finally comes, the word that stops them is the first one. I was raised without a father, and I know what that word can do. For people raised that way it can carry nothing at all, or it can carry a particular ache you learn to walk around, the way you learn the layout of a dark room so you never have to turn on the light. So we'll begin where the prayer begins, and we'll go slowly. The question isn't whether these words are familiar. Of course they are. The question is whether we've ever heard the opening line, or whether we've said it so often that one of the most astonishing things Jesus ever said about God has gone quiet in our mouths.

Luke tells us how the prayer came to be given. One of the disciples said, "Lord, teach us to pray, as John taught his disciples" (Luke 11:1). The first word Jesus gives them in answer is a family word. Later, in Gethsemane, in the worst hour of his life, he prays, "Abba, Father, all things are possible for you" (Mark 14:36). Abba is Aramaic, the word of a child to a parent, a word from the home more than the temple. The German scholar Joachim Jeremias argued that no Jewish prayer before Jesus addressed God with that word. Later scholars, James Barr chief among them in a 1988 essay, corrected the popular idea that grew up around this, that Abba simply means "Daddy." Barr was right to correct it. But the wonder survives the correction. Whatever the exact warmth of the word, Jesus took his own closeness with the Father and handed it to fishermen and tax collectors. Paul says the Spirit now puts the same cry in our mouths: "you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" (Romans 8:15). That's why the fatherless can pray it as truly as anyone. The word isn't something we work up. It's given.

But there's something the sentimental reading misses every time, and I have to name it because so many of us have fallen into it. The line doesn't stop at Father. "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name" (Matthew 6:9). The same short breath that brings God close holds him in awe. Hallowed means treated as holy, set apart. It's the holiness Isaiah met when the seraphim covered their faces and called to one another, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" (Isaiah 6:3), and the prophet came apart: "Woe is me! For I am lost" (Isaiah 6:5).

I want to be fair to the God many of us now picture, because there's something true in him. Our age recovered God's nearness, and that recovery healed a real wound. There was a coldness in some older religion, a God held so high and far away that people could fear him but not love him. A God who runs to meet the prodigal son is the God of the Bible, and anyone who learned that late knows it as rescue. But watch what happened when the nearness kept growing and the holiness drained away. We ended up with a God whose whole job is to affirm us, a friend who agrees with whatever we already wanted. That isn't the Father Jesus reveals. It's our own need with a Bible verse taped to it. The sociologist Christian Smith gave the American version a name, moralistic therapeutic deism: a God who wants us nice and happy and asks nothing holy of us. It's a Father with the hallowed taken out.

None of us stands outside this. Many of us pray the word Father for years before we can feel that it means anything, saying it into what seems like an empty room, minds on the calendar, hearts a few steps behind our mouths. We treat God as a comfort we can call up and forget that he's a fire. We want the Abba without the hallowed. I've done it, and I suspect you have too.

Here is the gift of the line. The prayer doesn't ask us to choose. It doesn't offer a tender God or a holy God and make us pick. It holds them together in a handful of words and gives them to us whole, so that the God I'm invited to approach like a child climbing into a lap is the God whose name I'm not fit to speak. A man raised without a father is given a Father, and the Father he's given is the Holy One. Both are true in the same breath. Only the Son, who knew that Father from the inside, could have taught us to pray this way.

scriptureStudy.note: "Pray then like this: 'Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.'" The address is already teaching. Father is closeness, in heaven is transcendence, and hallowed is holiness. The prayer won't let us keep one without the other two.

"Abba, Father, all things are possible for you. Remove this cup from me." Jesus prays this word in agony. Abba isn't a fair-weather word. It's what the Son says to the Father when everything is falling apart.

"You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, 'Abba! Father!'" The word Jesus used is now placed in our mouths by the Spirit, so calling God Abba isn't presumption. It's the evidence of adoption.

"And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, 'Abba! Father!'" The closeness is given, not generated. The Spirit of the Son teaches us the Son's own word, which is why the fatherless can pray it as truly as anyone.

"Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of hosts; the whole earth is full of his glory!" This is what hallowed reaches for, the holiness before which the seraphim cover their faces. The prayer that says Father is addressed to this God, not a safer one.

"And I will vindicate the holiness of my great name, which has been profaned among the nations." To pray "hallowed be your name" is to ask for what God has already promised to do, so the first petition lines us up with God's own purpose before it asks anything for us.

"If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!" Jesus makes the heavenly Father the original and every human father the dim copy.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how seriously the early church took this opening line. Tertullian, writing on prayer around AD 200, called the Lord's Prayer a summary of the whole gospel. Cyprian of Carthage, writing his own treatise on it about fifty years later, lingered on the boldness of calling God Father, and warned that someone who calls God Father ought to live as one of his children. In the fourth century the prayer was taught to new believers as they came to baptism, as something that belonged to the adopted.

Then weigh the scholarly argument over Abba. Jeremias recovered the closeness of the word; Barr in 1988 corrected the popular overreach that turned it into a nursery word. The truth sits between them: a closeness that is real and deep without being cheap. Finally, take the harder turn into our own time. The philosopher Charles Taylor has traced how the modern West came to live inside what he calls the immanent frame, a world that runs without reference to God, where faith survives, if at all, as one option among others. Christian Smith's moralistic therapeutic deism describes what that does to belief in the pews. Ask the group whether their own picture of God has more of the cold distance of the old error or the soft nearness of the new one. The aim isn't to swing back into a distant God, which was its own mistake, but to recover the whole line.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group grew up with a father who was harsh and unpredictable. She says quietly, and with real pain, that she can't pray the word Father. It closes her throat. Every time she says it she sees the wrong face. She isn't being difficult, and she isn't in unbelief. She's telling the truth about a wound.

Honor the wound before you say anything else. Don't hurry her toward a correction, and don't treat the difficulty as weak faith, because that would only confirm that the word Father is a place of judgment. If what she describes is abuse, make sure she knows about the help information printed with this guide and that you're available to talk privately. Then, gently, you might point out what the prayer is doing. It isn't asking her to feel warmly toward her earthly father. It's offering her a different Father entirely. Jesus treats every human father as a copy at best, and some copies are a lie about the original.

Don't force the word into her mouth. Let her lean on the group's prayers until the word becomes hers. Use this to ask the room where their own picture of God was drawn by someone who wasn't God, and what it would take to let Jesus redraw it.

memoryVerse.text: Pray then like this: Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name.

sessions.title: Your Kingdom Come, Your Will Be Done
sessions.aim: To see that the prayer asks for God's kingdom and God's will before it mentions our own needs, to feel what it costs to pray against our own preferences, and to find in Gethsemane a will surrendered in trust rather than in defeat.
sessions.summary:
"Your will be done" (Matthew 6:10) may be the most dangerous sentence in the prayer, and we say it without thinking. We treat it as a sigh of resignation, the thing you murmur when you've run out of options. Jesus put it near the front of the prayer, before bread and before forgiveness, and meant it as the daily surrender of the thing we guard hardest, our own way.

To pray "your kingdom come" is to ask for the end of every rival kingdom, including the small, comfortable one where we sit on the throne. Jesus prayed these words for real in Gethsemane: "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). He named what he wanted and then laid it down.

There's a serious objection here, and the church has earned it. "Your will be done" has been used to tell the suffering and the oppressed to stop struggling. But the kingdom Jesus announced isn't passive. It brings down the mighty and fills the hungry. Praying for it makes a person restless for the world God intends. And surrender isn't the death of desire. It's desire aimed at last at something good enough to hold it.

keyScripture.why: "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me. Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). Jesus prays the petition for real in his worst hour, naming what he wants and then surrendering it. That's the pattern for every "your will be done."

discussion.q: What's the difference between resigning yourself to God's will and surrendering to it? Have you known both?
discussion.behind: This distinction runs through the whole session. Resignation is the shrug of someone who has given up because nothing can be done. Surrender is trust, laying down what you wanted into hands you believe are good. The same words can be either, and the difference matters a great deal.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 6:9-13. The prayer asks for God's name, kingdom and will before it asks for our bread. Why do you think Jesus ordered it that way, and what does it say about us that we'd have put our needs first?
discussion.behind: The order is part of the teaching. We'd have written the prayer starting with requests. Our needs matter, but they find their right place once God is in his. Help the room hear this as relief, not rebuke.

discussion.q: To pray "your kingdom come" is to pray for the end of every rival kingdom, including the small one where you sit on the throne. What does your small kingdom look like, and what would it cost to pray for its end?
discussion.behind: Everyone has built a small domain arranged around their own comfort and preference. Help each person name theirs without shaming them, and let the cost be real. A prayer that costs nothing changes nothing.

discussion.q: "Your will be done" has been used to tell suffering people to stop struggling. What is true in that charge, and how is the kingdom Jesus announced the opposite of passive? (See Luke 1:52-53.)
discussion.behind: Grant the charge fully, and be careful with anyone in the room who has had the line used on them. Then show that Jesus' kingdom comes against the powers, feeding, healing and overturning, so praying for it is about the least passive thing a person can do.

discussion.q: In Gethsemane Jesus said what he wanted before he said "nevertheless." What does it mean that surrender didn't require him to pretend he wanted the cross?
discussion.behind: Close on the relief in this. Surrender isn't pretending you have no desire. It's bringing the real desire to the surface and then laying it down. People don't have to fake wanting God's will. They can say what they actually want and then, like Jesus, add the nevertheless.

objections.objection: Praying "your will be done" makes people passive. It teaches them to accept suffering, injustice and abuse as God's plan instead of fighting to change what's wrong. Religion uses it to keep people quiet.
objections.response: This charge lands on real history, so don't soften it. The church has told slaves to obey their masters as though that settled the matter, told women in violent homes that their suffering was a cross to bear, and told the poor their poverty was God's will. Every one of those was a lie told in God's name. Where suffering can be relieved and injustice resisted, hiding behind "your will be done" isn't faith. It's cowardice with a pious accent. But the objection assumes the kingdom Jesus prayed for is a kingdom of acceptance, and it's the reverse. Mary sang that God "has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty" (Luke 1:52-53). To pray "your kingdom come" is to ask for exactly the overturning the objection cares about. Passivity doesn't pray for a kingdom to come. It prays for nothing to change. If anyone hearing this is being harmed at home, the help information printed with this guide is for them, and God's will is their safety.

objections.objection: If God's will is going to be done anyway, praying for it is pointless. Either he's in control and my prayer changes nothing, or my prayer matters and he isn't really in control. You can't have both.
objections.response: It's a real puzzle, not a cheap dodge, and Christians have argued about it for centuries. Notice the assumption, though: that prayer exists to inform God or change his mind, like a lever that moves an outcome. Jesus doesn't teach prayer that way. In this petition, prayer is how we're drawn into God's purposes. "Your will be done" is less a request that God do something than a surrender in which we're changed from people resisting his will into people who want it. John Calvin, in his long treatment of prayer, answered the objection by saying that God appoints the means along with the end, and that prayer is one of the means. On that view prayer is a real cause with real effects, not because it overpowers God but because he has chosen to work through his children's asking. Christians weigh that differently, and the group doesn't need to settle it tonight. What everyone can see is Gethsemane, where the cup didn't pass but the one praying walked out ready to drink it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the one thing you haven't been willing to say "your will be done" about, the cup you keep asking to pass without ever reaching the nevertheless?
sessions.practice: This week, find the one place where you've been praying for your own will and calling it God's. Bring it into the light. Say what you actually want, out loud, the way Jesus named the cup, without pretending you want something else. Then, and only then, add the second half: "nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." Don't force the feeling. Just say the sentence. Write down what the second half costs you, and whether saying it loosens the grip of the first.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven. We've said these words as a sigh of defeat when you meant them as an act of trust. Forgive the small kingdoms we've built with ourselves on the throne, and the prayers we've prayed for our own way while saying yours. Teach us to want your kingdom more than our comfort, and to bring our real desires into the open before we lay them down. Give us the courage of Gethsemane, to name the cup and then to say nevertheless. Where there's injustice we could resist, don't let us hide behind your name. Make us restless for the world you intend. Amen.
reflection: Where have I been praying for my own will and calling it God's?
What small kingdom have I built with myself at the center, and can I pray for its end?
Have I confused surrender with resignation, giving up because I felt I had no choice rather than laying something down in trust?
sessions.teaching:
"Your will be done" (Matthew 6:10) may be the most dangerous sentence in the prayer, and most of us say it without thinking. We've turned it into a sigh of resignation, the thing you murmur at a hospital bed when the options have run out, the noise you make when you've already lost. That isn't where Jesus put it, and it isn't what he meant by it. He placed it near the front of the prayer, before the bread, before the forgiveness, before a single one of our needs gets a word, and he meant it as a daily surrender of the one possession we guard hardest, our own way. There's a version of these words that costs nothing and a version that costs everything, and only one of them is the prayer Jesus taught.

Start with the petition just before it, "your kingdom come," because the two belong together. This isn't a vague wish for heaven someday. Jesus began his preaching by saying, "The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel" (Mark 1:15). The kingdom is God's reign breaking into this world now, and to ask for it is also to ask for the end of every rival kingdom. Here's the part we skip. The most stubborn rival kingdom usually isn't in a capital city. It's the small, comfortable, well-defended kingdom we've built with ourselves on the throne, where our preferences are law and every person and circumstance gets judged by whether it serves us. "Your kingdom come" is a prayer for that kingdom to fall. No wonder we say it quickly.

Now the strongest case against all this, and the people who make it are often people who have been hurt. They say "your will be done" breeds passivity, that a religion built on it produces people who accept injustice and call it godliness, who tell the suffering to stop struggling and the oppressed to wait for the next world. On the history, they're right. The church has told slaves that their chains were God's will. It has told women in violent homes that their suffering was a cross to bear. It has blessed the arrangements of the powerful and handed the powerless a prayer to keep them quiet. That isn't the gospel. It's the gospel turned against the very people it came to free, and it should make us angry.

But the objection misses something about the kingdom itself, and everything turns on it. The kingdom Jesus announced isn't a kingdom of acceptance. It comes against the powers. Mary sang of a God who "has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things, and the rich he has sent away empty" (Luke 1:52-53). Praying for that kingdom is about the least passive thing a person can do. It makes you restless, unable to make peace with the way things are, because you've started praying for the way things ought to be. And Jesus won't let the prayer stay on our lips: "Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven" (Matthew 7:21). Praying the will and doing it are meant to be one thing.

Then Gethsemane, because Jesus didn't teach this from a safe distance. He prayed it in a garden in the dark, and Luke says "his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground" (Luke 22:44). Look at how he prayed: he didn't pretend. He didn't put on a calm he didn't feel and announce that he'd wanted the cross all along. He said, "Father, if you are willing, remove this cup from me." He named what he wanted and held nothing back. Then he said the second half: "Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done" (Luke 22:42). That's the pattern, and there's relief hidden in it. Surrender isn't pretending you want what you don't want. It's naming the cup and then laying it down into hands you've decided to trust.

Most of us have prayed for our own will for most of our lives while our mouths said his. I know I have. We've arranged a life around our own comfort and called the arrangement wisdom. We've prayed "your will be done" at the very moments we'd already made sure our will would be done, using the prayer to decorate a decision. And it has never made us free. It has made us anxious and small and tired from guarding a kingdom that was never worth the guard. The freedom is on the other side of the nevertheless. "Your will be done" isn't where desire dies. It's where desire finally finds something good enough to hold it.

scriptureStudy.note: "Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven." The two petitions are one movement. They ask that God's reign and will, already perfect in heaven, break into earth, which is a prayer for the world to be remade and not merely endured.
"Nevertheless, not my will, but yours, be done." Jesus prays the petition for real. The model isn't suppressed desire but surrendered desire, the cup named and then laid down.

"My Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me; nevertheless, not as I will, but as you will." Matthew says he fell on his face. Both the posture and the candor are complete, and both sit inside a surrender that doesn't pretend the cross was easy.

"He has brought down the mighty from their thrones and exalted those of humble estate; he has filled the hungry with good things." Mary's song describes the kingdom we pray to come. It overturns the world's order, so praying for it is praying for justice, not for quiet.

"The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God is at hand; repent and believe in the gospel." The kingdom is already breaking in, which is why we pray for it in the present tense, for something here and not yet fully here.

"Not everyone who says to me, 'Lord, Lord,' will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven." Praying the will and doing it belong together, so the petition commits us to obedience, not only to acceptance.

"And this is the confidence that we have toward him, that if we ask anything according to his will he hears us." Confidence in prayer is tied to asking according to his will, which is what this petition trains us to want.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, take up the old question this petition raises: how God's sovereign will and our prayers fit together. John Calvin gave his fullest treatment of prayer in the third book of his Institutes, chapter 20, and much of it is an exposition of the Lord's Prayer. He faced the objection that prayer is pointless if God has already decided the end, and answered that God ordains the means along with the end and has appointed prayer as one of those means. Not every Christian tradition puts it that way, and a group can weigh other answers too. Whatever you conclude, notice what happens in Gethsemane. The surrender doesn't change the outcome; the cup doesn't pass. It changes the one praying, who leaves the garden ready to carry what he asked to be spared.

Then press the pastoral edge. Our culture tends to treat our own desires as the one thing we must never surrender, which makes this petition almost unintelligible to modern ears. Ask the group where they've heard that their wants are sovereign, and whether believing it has made them freer. The aim is to recover "your will be done" not as the sigh of people who've given up, but as the trusting act of people who've decided God's will is better than their own.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is going through real suffering, an illness or a loss. When the session turns to "your will be done," he goes quiet and then says, with an edge, that he's tired of being told to accept it. Everyone keeps quoting this line at him as though his job is to stop wanting things to be different. He isn't wrong to be angry.

Don't quote the petition at him the way others have. Honor the anger, and then give him Gethsemane, which is the opposite of the resignation being pressed on him. Jesus, facing his own suffering, didn't pretend to want it. He said plainly, "remove this cup from me" (Luke 22:42). Wanting things to be different isn't a failure of faith; it's in the prayer, on the Lord's own lips. What he's being invited to is not to stop wanting relief, but to bring the wanting to a Father he can trust, and in time, on no one else's schedule, to reach the nevertheless.

Don't rush him to the second half. Let him live in the first half as long as he needs. Ask the group where they've pushed someone toward acceptance because the other person's pain made them uncomfortable.

memoryVerse.text: Your kingdom come, your will be done, on earth as it is in heaven.

sessions.title: Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread
sessions.aim: To recover the smallness and candor of asking God for bread, to see daily dependence as the cure for both anxiety and self-sufficiency, and to learn from the manna what it means to ask for enough rather than for more.
sessions.summary:
The strangest thing about this petition is how small it is. After God's name, kingdom and will, the prayer turns and asks for bread, for one day, and nothing more: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). Dependence turns out not to be a lower thing than worship. It's a form of it. To ask God for bread is to admit every day that you didn't make yourself and can't keep yourself.

The word translated "daily," epiousios, is so rare that Origen, writing on prayer in the third century, said he could find it in no other Greek writer and thought the Gospel writers had coined it. Scholars still argue about its exact sense, but it points to bread for the day, not for the storehouse.

There's a fair objection: in a world of mortgages and retirement accounts, asking only for today sounds naive. Scripture praises the ant that stores up food. But the petition isn't against planning. It's against the anxiety planning becomes when we forget who provides. In the wilderness, the manna Israel hoarded "bred worms and stank" (Exodus 16:20). We ask for more because we think enough will finally make us safe. It never has. The one who learns to pray for daily bread is learning the freedom of enough.

keyScripture.why: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11). The request admits we didn't make ourselves and can't keep ourselves, and it trains us to ask for enough for today rather than for the security of a full barn.

discussion.q: After the kingdom of God, the prayer asks for bread. Why do you think Jesus put such an ordinary request in the middle of such a sacred prayer?
discussion.behind: Open on the surprise. We expect the prayer to stay lofty, and it asks for lunch. The ordinariness is the point: God cares about bread, and dependence in small things isn't beneath him. The petition won't separate the spiritual from the material.

discussion.q: To ask God for bread is to admit you didn't make yourself and can't keep yourself. Where in your life have you quietly stopped admitting that, living as though your provision came from your own hand?
discussion.behind: Most of us, especially the capable and comfortable, thank God with our mouths and trust our paycheck with our hands. Help people find the place they've stopped depending, and don't shame the responsible. The issue is where the heart rests, not the size of the account.

discussion.q: Read Exodus 16:4 and 16:19-20. What was God teaching Israel with bread that couldn't be stored, and what would change if you asked for enough for today instead of security for tomorrow?
discussion.behind: The manna is the picture under the petition: enough for today, gathered again tomorrow. Help the room notice how much anxiety comes from trying to secure a future we can't see. The petition is a discipline of the present.

discussion.q: Someone might say that asking only for today is naive in a world of mortgages and retirement accounts. What's true in that, and where does wise planning cross over into anxious hoarding?
discussion.behind: Grant it fully. Scripture praises the ant that stores (Proverbs 6:6-8), and the petition isn't against providing for a family. Then name the line: the point where planning stops being wisdom and becomes an attempt to make yourself safe apart from God.

discussion.q: Is there an amount you've quietly decided would finally be enough to feel safe? Has reaching for it ever actually quieted the fear?
discussion.behind: Close on the freedom in this. The lie is that a little more will finally be enough, and it never delivers, because the fear was never about the amount. Let it land as freedom, not as a rule against saving. Answer it yourself first, briefly.

objections.objection: Praying for daily bread is a luxury of the comfortable. Tell it to the child who starved yesterday despite every prayer. If God gives daily bread, why do millions go without while people who never pray have full tables?
objections.response: Don't rush past this. It's the hardest thing anyone will say about this petition, and it deserves more than a slogan. People pray for bread and don't receive it, children starve, and no tidy answer should be offered to a grief that size. Anyone who uses this petition to suggest the hungry didn't pray hard enough has understood neither the prayer nor the God who taught it. But notice two things. First, the prayer says "give us," not "give me," and the us includes the hungry. To pray it truthfully is to be drafted into God's provision for the poor, to become one of the ways the bread arrives, and that convicts every full table that prayed the words and did nothing. Very often bread fails to reach the hungry not because God withholds it but because the well-fed keep it. Second, the prayer teaches us to receive our own bread as a gift, not a wage, and someone who knows his bread is a gift can't look at a hungry neighbor and call the difference deserved. The petition doesn't explain all hunger. It commits the one who prays it to fight it.

objections.objection: This teaches people to be careless, to skip saving and planning and expect God to drop food from the sky. God helps those who help themselves.
objections.response: Start with the proverb, gently. "God helps those who help themselves" isn't in the Bible. It's an old saying that goes back to Aesop's gods and was made famous in America by Benjamin Franklin, and it says nearly the opposite of the gospel, which is that God helps those who can't help themselves. Then grant what's true in the concern. Scripture praises foresight: "Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Proverbs 6:6). This petition isn't a command to quit your job and wait for manna. But planning and dependence aren't opposites. A farmer plants and waters and then waits on rain he can't make, and both the work and the waiting are real. The petition doesn't forbid the barn. It forbids the barn becoming your god, the moment your security moves from the Father who gives to the barn you've filled. That's the rich man in Jesus' parable who built bigger barns and died the night he finished them (Luke 12:18-20). Plan carefully, and pray knowing that it always depended on God.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: What's the amount you've quietly decided would finally be enough to feel safe, and what would it mean to admit that the number has kept moving your whole life?
sessions.practice: This week, before you eat, stop and ask God for the food already in front of you, out loud if you can, as a real request and not a formality. Notice how strange it feels to ask for what you assumed you'd earned. Then, once this week, give some of your bread away to someone who doesn't have enough, because the prayer says "give us," not "give me." Write down what you notice about your own idea of enough, and whether asking daily loosens its grip.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, give us this day our daily bread. We live as though we made ourselves, as though the breath in our lungs and the food on our tables came from our own hands, and we've forgotten how to ask you for anything because we assumed we'd earned it. Teach us to receive our bread as a gift and not a wage. Free us from the lie that a little more will finally make us safe. And because this prayer says give us and not give me, make us the hands by which the hungry are fed, and don't let us pray for bread at full tables while our neighbor goes without. Give us enough today, and the freedom enough has always been. Amen.
reflection: Where have I stopped depending on God, living as the provider of my own security?
What number have I decided would finally be enough, and has reaching for it ever quieted the fear underneath?
The prayer says give us, not give me. Whose hunger have I been treating as none of my concern?
sessions.teaching:
The strangest thing about this petition is how small it is. Look at where the prayer has just been: the name of God, hallowed; the kingdom of God, asked to come; the will of God, done on earth as in heaven. The horizon has been the whole creation. Then the prayer turns a corner and asks for bread. Not for the meaning of life, not for the salvation of the soul, but for something to eat today: "Give us this day our daily bread" (Matthew 6:11).

Why would Jesus put such an ordinary request in such a sacred prayer? We tend to think dependence is a lower thing than worship, a distraction from the real business of praise. It isn't. Asking God for bread may be among the most truthful acts of worship we have, because it admits out loud, every day, that you didn't make yourself and you can't keep yourself, that the life you walk around assuming is yours is a gift you're receiving from a hand that isn't your own. Capable people dislike this. Dependence feels like weakness, and many of us have built lives designed to need no one, least of all a God we can't see. Jesus hands us a prayer that won't let us pretend.

The word itself repays a closer look. The Greek word translated "daily" is epiousios. Origen, writing his treatise on prayer in the third century, said he couldn't find it in any other Greek writer and concluded that the Gospel writers had coined it for this prayer. Scholars have argued about its exact sense ever since: bread for our existence, bread for the coming day, tomorrow's bread given today. But through all the debate the direction is clear. It asks for bread for the day. Not for the year, not for the storehouse. For today, and then tomorrow, for that day.

Now take the strongest case against this, because a reasonable person will make it. In a world of mortgages and retirement accounts and children to put through school, asking God only for today sounds naive at best. Prudence thinks about tomorrow. Scripture itself says, "Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways, and be wise" (Proverbs 6:6), and praises the woman who provides for her household and "laughs at the time to come" (Proverbs 31:25). Grant all of it. This petition isn't a command to stop planning or empty the savings account. God isn't against the barn.

But there's a real line where the barn turns from wisdom into an idol. It's the moment your security quietly moves, when it stops resting in the Father who provides and starts resting in the pile you've gathered, so your peace rises and falls with the number. Jesus told a story about a rich man who said, "I will tear down my barns and build larger ones," and planned to tell his soul, "relax, eat, drink, be merry." "But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you'" (Luke 12:18-20). He wasn't condemned for planning. He was condemned for trusting the plan instead of the one who provides, for building a security with no room for God in it.

The manna is the picture under the whole petition. In the wilderness God fed Israel with bread from heaven, and the instruction was exact: "the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day" (Exodus 16:4). Some didn't trust it. They kept extra overnight against the fear of tomorrow, "and it bred worms and stank" (Exodus 16:20). The lesson wasn't that saving is sin. It was that God meant to be trusted daily, that dependence wasn't a phase to outgrow but the permanent shape of a creature's life before its Creator.

Most of us pray "give us this day our daily bread" and then lie awake working out tomorrow. I do. We believe, without ever saying it, that a little more would finally be the amount that made us safe, and we watch the number move every time we get close, because the fear was never really about money. We ask for more because we think enough will finally make us safe. It never has. Jesus points past the loaf to himself: "I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger" (John 6:35). He doesn't despise the literal bread. He tells us who is behind it. The person who has learned to pray for daily bread, and mean it, has found a freedom the anxious can't buy, the rest of someone who asks for today, receives it as a gift, and trusts the Father for a tomorrow they were never going to secure anyway.

scriptureStudy.note: "Give us this day our daily bread." The petition is plural and present, our bread and this day, teaching a dependence that's shared with others and renewed every morning.

"Behold, I am about to rain bread from heaven for you, and the people shall go out and gather a day's portion every day." The manna sets the pattern the petition assumes, training Israel to depend on God morning by morning.
"But they did not listen to Moses. Some left part of it till the morning, and it bred worms and stank." Hoarded manna rotting is the picture of security sought apart from daily trust.

"Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the food that is needful for me, lest I be full and deny you." Agur asks for exactly enough, seeing that too much and too little both endanger the soul.

"I will tear down my barns and build larger ones... But God said to him, 'Fool! This night your soul is required of you.'" The rich man isn't condemned for planning but for trusting the plan instead of the Provider.

"Therefore do not be anxious, saying, 'What shall we eat?'... But seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you." In the same sermon, Jesus puts the kingdom first and the bread after, the same order as the prayer.
"I am the bread of life; whoever comes to me shall not hunger." Jesus points past the loaf to himself, so asking for daily bread trains a deeper hunger, without ever despising the literal loaf.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how the church has heard more in the word bread than the stomach alone. Early readers, Origen and later Augustine among them, took daily bread to include the bread of the word and of the Lord's Supper. The plain meaning is surely the ordinary loaf, but the instinct isn't wrong: the God who feeds the body feeds the soul. Weigh that against the opposite danger, the comfortable reader who quickly turns the bread into a metaphor so he doesn't have to think about the neighbor who lacks the literal kind.

Then bring in what the secular world has noticed. Researchers who study money and happiness describe what they call the hedonic treadmill: once real needs are met, more tends not to bring the security it promises, because we adjust and want more again. That gets the symptom right. It can't supply the cure, which isn't a technique for contentment but a Father to depend on. Finally, take up the plural. Cyprian of Carthage noticed in the third century that we're taught to say "our" and "us," so the Christian never prays for bread alone but always for the whole body. Ask the group what it would mean in their own church and town to pray "give us" and mean it.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a man in your group is a careful saver and planner, quietly proud of the security he's built for his family. When the session turns to daily bread and the danger of the barn, he bristles. He says he doesn't see the problem: he's worked hard, providing for his household is a biblical duty, and he resents the suggestion that his savings account is an idol.

Honor him before you press him, because he's right about the duty. Scripture commends providing for one's family, and his diligence is a real good. Say so and mean it. But notice the bristle. The petition doesn't condemn the barn. It asks where his security actually rests, and the real test isn't the size of the account but what happens in him when the account is threatened. You might ask, kindly, whether he could pray "give us this day" and mean the "this day."

Use this to ask the whole group the same question. Most of us have some barn. The question isn't whether we have one but whether we built it so we'd never have to ask again.

memoryVerse.text: Give us this day our daily bread.

sessions.title: Forgive Us Our Debts, As We Forgive
sessions.aim: To face the small word as, to see that Jesus binds the forgiveness we receive to the forgiveness we give, and to find that this isn't a threat against grace but the sign that grace has actually landed, while refusing every use of the petition against the wounded.
sessions.summary:
There's one word in this prayer that should stop us every time, and we read right over it because it's small. "Forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). Not because we forgive, and not so that we'll learn to. As. By the same measure. And the moment the prayer ends, Jesus comes back to this petition alone: "if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Matthew 6:15).

Serious Christians worry that this makes forgiveness something we earn, and they're guarding something true. We aren't saved by our forgiving. But softening the word as into nothing means deleting what Jesus plainly said and the parable he told to explain it: the servant forgiven a debt he could never pay who then seizes a fellow servant by the throat over a small one (Matthew 18:23-35). Our forgiving doesn't buy God's. A person who has received an ocean of mercy and refuses a cupful has shown he never understood what he received.

This petition has also been used as a whip against the wounded. Forgiveness isn't excusing, forgetting, or going back within reach of someone who is still doing harm. It's the slow release of the right to make someone pay, and it never runs on anyone else's timeline.

keyScripture.why: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). The mercy we ask from God is bound to the mercy we give, not as payment for grace but as the sign that grace has taken hold.

discussion.q: Say the petition slowly together: "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." What happens in you when you actually hear the measure you're asking God to use?
discussion.behind: Most people have prayed this a thousand times without hearing the word as. Don't resolve the theology yet. Let the weight land first: we're asking God to measure his mercy to us by ours to others.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 6:14-15. Of all the petitions, Jesus comes back to this one the moment the prayer ends. Why do you think forgiveness carries this condition?
discussion.behind: Forgiveness is the one place where the mercy we've received and the mercy we give meet in the same person, so it's the clearest test of whether the grace was real. Jesus isn't being harsh. He's showing whether we understood what we were given.

discussion.q: Some Christians worry that this makes forgiveness earned. What is that worry rightly protecting, and what happens if we soften the word as until it means nothing?
discussion.behind: Hold both halves. The worry is right: we aren't saved by our forgiving, and a reading that makes mercy a wage is a false gospel. But the soft reading has to erase Jesus' plain words and the parable that explains them. Help the room hold the tension: not earned, and not optional, the fruit that shows the root.

discussion.q: Read Matthew 18:23-35. Where are you the first servant, holding a small debt against someone while standing forgiven a huge one?
discussion.behind: Everyone is holding something. Help people set their small debt beside the one they've been forgiven. Go first if the room is slow, and keep it concrete. If someone names real abuse, don't treat it as a small debt; see the case study and the help information printed with this guide.

discussion.q: How does remembering the size of your own forgiven debt change your grip on the one you're holding?
discussion.behind: Close on grace. The cure for unforgiveness isn't trying harder; it's remembering how much you've been forgiven until the difference loosens the grip. Grace first, then the command, always.

objections.objection: This makes forgiveness a transaction. If God only forgives me when I forgive others, then salvation is earned by my behavior, and grace collapses into another religion of works.
objections.response: This worry is guarding something precious, so take it seriously. We aren't saved by our forgiving. If the word as meant that my mercy purchases God's, the gospel really would collapse into a wage system, and nobody would be saved, because nobody forgives perfectly. Hold that line. But the same worry, pushed too far, has to delete Jesus' plainest words on the subject: "if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Matthew 6:15). It also has to explain away the parable of the unforgiving servant, whose master hands him to the jailers for refusing to show the mercy he'd been shown (Matthew 18:34). Jesus isn't describing a purchase. He's describing something that can't be held together: receiving an ocean of forgiveness and then keeping a cupful back from your neighbor. Refusing to forgive isn't failing to pay a price. It's evidence that the mercy never reached the heart. The forgiven forgive, not to earn what they were given but because they have it.

objections.objection: Telling victims they have to forgive is cruel. It lets abusers off the hook and makes the wounded excuse what was done to them. This petition has been used to silence people and keep them in harm.
objections.response: Don't defend that misuse for a moment. This petition has been used to tell the battered and betrayed that their healing depends on excusing the one who hurt them, and that's a cruelty the prayer never sponsored. Say so plainly first. Then clear up the definition the misuse depends on. Forgiveness isn't saying the wrong wasn't wrong. It isn't excusing, forgetting or pretending, and it is never going back within reach of someone who is still doing harm. Forgiveness is the release of your right to make the other person pay, and you can let go of that while still naming the wrong, refusing to be harmed again, and pursuing justice and safety, including going to the authorities. Forgiving someone doesn't mean trusting them or returning to them. Reconciliation needs the offender's repentance and is sometimes impossible. Forgiveness is something God works in the wounded, often slowly, so that what was done no longer owns them, and it is never demanded of a bleeding person on someone else's timeline. Where someone is in danger, the first thing is safety, and the help information printed with this guide says where to find it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Whose debt are you holding right now, kept ready to bring out, and what does keeping it let you feel that letting it go would cost you?
sessions.practice: This week, name one person you haven't forgiven. Before you try to forgive them, sit with the size of what God has forgiven you. Then, only if you can, tell God you're releasing the debt: not excusing the wrong, not going back to harm, but letting go of your right to make them pay. If the wound is very deep, or the person is still dangerous, don't force it. Bring it to God as it is, talk to the leader, and use the help information printed with this guide. Write down what rises in you when you set your small debt beside your forgiven one.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors. We say these words quickly because we don't dare hear them. Forgive us again, and this time let your mercy reach all the way down, to the place where we're still holding something back from someone who wronged us. Remind us what we've been forgiven until the grip loosens. And where the wound is deep, where someone here has been told that healing means excusing what was done to them, teach the forgiveness that lets go of the debt without going back to the harm. Give safety, and patience, and time. We forgive because you forgave us first. Amen.
reflection: What debt am I holding, and have I ever set it beside the size of the debt God forgave me?
Have I softened the word as until it stopped meaning anything, so I wouldn't have to forgive?
Is my unforgiveness a sign that I'm owed something, or a sign that I've forgotten what I was given?
sessions.teaching:
There's one word in the Lord's Prayer that should stop us every time, and the reason it doesn't is that it's small and we read right over it. "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors" (Matthew 6:12). Jesus didn't say "forgive us because we've forgiven," as though our mercy earned his. He didn't say "forgive us so that we can learn to forgive," as though ours were simply the result. He said as. By the same measure, with the same ruler we've been using on everyone who has wronged us. In the middle of the only prayer he taught, we're asking God to forgive us the way we forgive other people. Read it again and notice how much of us would rather he didn't.

The word "debts" matters too. Sin is described as something owed, an obligation we can't pay. And Jesus seems to know we'll try to slip out of the as, because the moment the prayer is finished he comes back to it: "For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Matthew 6:14-15). He doesn't comment on the bread or expand on the kingdom. He returns to this one petition and presses it harder.

Now the strongest case for softening it, because faithful people make it and it protects something real. If God forgives me only on the condition that I forgive others, then salvation is something I earn by my behavior, and the gospel of grace collapses into another religion of works. There's real weight in that. We aren't saved by our forgiving. If we were, no one would be saved, because no one forgives perfectly, and the cross would become a down payment we finish paying off with our own mercy. Hold that line.

But to make the as mean nothing, you have to take a red pen to Jesus' plainest words, and you have to explain away the parable he told to explain this very petition. A servant owes his king "ten thousand talents" (Matthew 18:24), a sum so absurd it could never be repaid, and "out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt" (Matthew 18:27). Then the same servant goes out, finds a fellow servant who owes him a hundred denarii, a few months' wages, "and seizing him, he began to choke him, saying, 'Pay what you owe'" (Matthew 18:28). When he won't wait, he has the man put in prison. The king hears of it and says, "You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" (Matthew 18:32-33). There's the word again. As.

Listen to what Jesus is and isn't saying. The servant didn't purchase the king's mercy with his own; he'd already received it, freely, before he ever met his fellow servant. What Jesus is saying is that someone who has truly received an ocean of forgiveness and then clamps down on a cupful of it, refusing his neighbor the very thing that saved him, has shown by that refusal that he never understood what he was given. Unforgiveness isn't a failure to pay. It's a diagnosis. It reveals a heart that stood in a flood of mercy and somehow stayed dry. Paul puts the same order plainly: "as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive" (Colossians 3:13).

I have to say something carefully here, because this petition has been misused. It has been used as a whip on people who were abused or betrayed, telling them their healing depends on excusing what was done to them. That isn't what Jesus is teaching. Forgiveness isn't saying the wrong was fine. It isn't forgetting, and it is never going back within reach of someone who is still doing harm. It's the release, often slow, of the right to make the other person pay. You can do that while naming the wrong plainly, keeping yourself safe and seeking justice. Reconciliation is something else; it needs repentance from the one who did the harm, and sometimes it can't happen at all. If you're carrying a wound like that, nothing here asks you to call it acceptable, and the help information printed with this guide is there for you.

For most of us, though, the problem is closer to the first servant than we'd like. I pray "forgive me" in one breath and go over someone's offense against me in the next. We ask God for an ocean and give a neighbor a closed fist. We keep a debt filed and ready, bring it out in arguments, tend it in private, and tell ourselves we're owed. The unforgiveness we're nursing isn't evidence that we're owed something. It's evidence that we've forgotten what we were forgiven. Willpower has never opened that fist. What opens it is going back to stand in the size of our own forgiven debt, the whole unpayable weight of it taken at a cross we didn't carry, until it's no longer possible to keep choking someone over a hundred denarii while standing knee-deep in that much mercy. The as isn't a threat hanging over grace. It's the test of whether grace ever arrived.

scriptureStudy.note: "And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." Debts frames sin as something owed and unpayable. As binds the mercy we ask to the mercy we give, not as a purchase but as the measure that shows whether mercy was received.

"For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses." Jesus comes back to this petition alone, so we can't soften the as into nothing.

"One was brought to him who owed him ten thousand talents... And out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt." The sum is meant to be absurd, a debt no one could repay, so the mercy is total and free.

"But when that same servant went out, he found one of his fellow servants who owed him a hundred denarii, and seizing him, he began to choke him." The one just forgiven a fortune throttles a neighbor over a small debt, the picture of praying "forgive us" while refusing to forgive.

"You wicked servant! I forgave you all that debt because you pleaded with me. And should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?" He's condemned not for the original debt but for refusing to pass on the mercy he received.
"As the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive." Paul uses the same as. The forgiveness we received is both the model and the reason for the forgiveness we give.
"Be kind to one another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you." God's forgiveness in Christ comes first. Ours is the overflow, never the payment.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at how the Reformers handled this petition. They staked everything on salvation by grace alone, and yet they didn't soften the condition. They read it the way the parable does: the forgiveness we give is the fruit and evidence of faith, never its cause. The Heidelberg Catechism of 1563, in its answer on this petition, has us ask for forgiveness as people who, because of God's grace at work in us, are fully determined to forgive our neighbor from the heart. The order stays right: grace produces forgiveness, not the other way round.

Set beside that what researchers have found about forgiveness. A good deal of research suggests that resentment held for a long time harms the one who holds it, and that letting go of a grievance tends to bring relief. That gets the symptom right. It can describe the benefit of letting go without supplying the mercy that makes letting go possible. Then take the pastoral distinction between forgiveness and reconciliation. Forgiveness is the release of the debt, worked in the wounded for their freedom. Reconciliation needs the offender's repentance and can't be demanded or rushed. Where there's ongoing harm, the call is to safety. The aim is to keep the petition both grounded in grace and serious, refusing the reading that makes forgiveness a wage and the reading that makes it optional.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a woman in your group carries a deep wound, a betrayal or abuse from years ago. When the session turns to forgiveness she goes rigid and says, with quiet force, that she's been told her whole life she has to forgive, that people keep using this prayer to make her excuse what was done to her, and she's tired of it. She isn't being stubborn. She's protecting herself from a cruelty done to her in God's name.

Don't repeat that cruelty. Don't press the petition on her. You might name, plainly, that she's been wronged twice: once by the person who hurt her and again by everyone who used forgiveness as a whip. Then, gently, offer a different definition than the one she was handed. The forgiveness Jesus teaches isn't excusing the wrong or forgetting it, and it never means going back within reach of someone who is still doing harm. It's the eventual release of her right to make the person pay, worked slowly by God for her own freedom, and it doesn't require reconciliation with someone unrepentant or dangerous. There's no timeline she owes anyone.

If the harm is ongoing, or she's in danger, safety comes first. Make sure she has the help information printed with this guide, and offer to talk privately. Ask the rest of the group where they've used forgiveness to hurry someone else's pain along.

memoryVerse.text: And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors.

sessions.title: Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil
sessions.aim: To take seriously the last petition's plea for protection in the time of testing, to name the reality of evil the prayer won't explain away, and to end where the prayer ends, handing the kingdom, the power and the glory back to the God they always belonged to.
sessions.summary:
The prayer doesn't end in triumph. It ends with a request for rescue: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). It assumes we're weaker than we think and the danger is more real than we admit.

There's an old puzzle here. James says God "tempts no one" (James 1:13), so why ask God not to lead us into temptation? The Greek word, peirasmos, means testing or trial as much as enticement. The petition is best heard as a plea: don't let the testing be more than we can bear, don't leave us alone in the trial. In 2019 Pope Francis approved a new Italian wording of the line for the Mass, "do not abandon us to temptation," to guard against hearing God as the tempter.

The skeptic says evil is a primitive category, that what religion called the evil one is really psychology and circumstance. Some of that suspicion is earned. But the twentieth century, with its death camps and gulags, is a strange place to argue the word evil is naive. Then the doxology, missing from the oldest manuscripts of Matthew but prayed by the church since very early: "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever." The prayer that began by hallowing God's name ends by handing him everything we tried to keep. We finish smaller than we started, and that turns out to be where we're safe.

keyScripture.why: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). The last petition admits our weakness in the testing and our need of rescue from a real evil, so the prayer ends in dependence on the God who delivers, not in self-confidence.

discussion.q: We'd probably have ended the most important prayer on a note of victory. Jesus ends it with a plea for rescue. What is it like to finish with "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil"?
discussion.behind: Open on the humility of the ending. This isn't defeatism. It's truthfulness about the human condition. Sometimes the strongest thing we can do is admit we aren't strong enough and ask to be kept.

discussion.q: Read James 1:13 and 1 Corinthians 10:13. If God tempts no one, what are we asking for in this petition? Where have you needed God to spare you a trial you knew you couldn't get through on your own?
discussion.behind: Handle the puzzle with the plain reading: God may test his people, but he never entices anyone to evil. Then draw out the lived meaning. Asking to be spared, or kept, in a trial that feels beyond us is a humble and legitimate request, not a lack of faith.

discussion.q: Some people think evil is a primitive idea, that adults don't pray to be delivered from a devil. What's fair in that suspicion, and why might the twentieth century be a strange place to argue that the word evil is naive?
discussion.behind: Let the skeptic in the room feel understood before the turn. The suspicion is fair: the church has cried "devil" when the real problem was its own sin. Then press the counter. A century of industrialized murder makes the confident retirement of the word evil look less like maturity and more like forgetting.

discussion.q: The doxology hands God the kingdom, the power and the glory, the three things we spend our lives trying to keep. Which do you hold onto hardest: control, strength, or credit?
discussion.behind: Everyone grips one of the three. Help people name theirs and feel the release of handing it back. The doxology isn't flattering God; it's returning what was his.

discussion.q: The whole prayer has been making God larger and us smaller. How could being made smaller by this prayer be a rescue rather than a loss?
discussion.behind: Close on the arc of the study. The smallness isn't humiliation. It's setting down a weight we were never meant to carry. Let it end with weight, not a tidy bow.

objections.objection: Praying to be delivered from evil and the devil is superstition left over from a pre-scientific age. What people used to call evil we now understand as psychology, trauma and circumstance.
objections.response: Grant what the objection is reacting against, because the church has earned some of this suspicion. Evil has been used as a lazy explanation, a way to avoid examining our own hearts and our own systems, and the cry of "devil" has too often been aimed at inconvenient people rather than at wicked deeds. A healthy allergy to superstition is understandable. But watch the confidence of the claim, because it doesn't fit the record. The century that prided itself on outgrowing the category of evil produced the death camps, the gulags and the killing fields, murder on an industrial scale carried out by educated people with paperwork. Psychology and circumstance are real, and they explain a great deal, but they've never held the whole weight of that. Hannah Arendt, no believer in a devil, watched Adolf Eichmann's trial in Jerusalem and wrote of the banality of evil. She found the man ordinary, and she still called what he did evil. The petition doesn't require a cartoon devil with a pitchfork. It requires only the humility to admit there's a darkness in the world and in us that we didn't invent and can't master alone, and that the mature response is to ask to be delivered from it.

objections.objection: If I have to ask God not to lead me into temptation, then God must be the one tempting me. That makes God the author of my sin, which is monstrous.
objections.response: It's an old and serious puzzle, and the church has worked on it rather than waving it away. Start where James starts: "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God,' for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one" (James 1:13). Whatever the petition means, it can't mean God is the author of our sin. The key is the Greek word peirasmos, which means testing or trial as much as enticement. Read that way, the petition isn't accusing God of luring us. It's pleading about the trials that come: don't let the testing be more than we can bear, don't leave us alone in it. Paul gives the promise underneath: "God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape" (1 Corinthians 10:13). The concern is still alive. In 2019 Pope Francis approved a new Italian wording of this line for the Mass, roughly "do not abandon us to temptation," to guard against the misreading. God may test his children to strengthen them, but he never entices them to evil, and this petition asks the God who permits the trial to be the God who delivers us through it.

sessions.quietRoomQuestion: Which of the three, the kingdom, the power or the glory, have you spent your life trying to keep for yourself, and what has keeping it cost you?
sessions.practice: This week, pray the whole prayer through slowly, all the way to the end. Stop on the last petition long enough to ask, out loud, to be delivered from the particular trial and the particular evil you know is coming this week. Name it rather than praying in general. Then, at the doxology, hand God the one of the three you hold hardest, the control, the strength or the credit, saying it back to him as his. Write down what it feels like to end the prayer smaller than you began, and whether the smallness felt like loss or like rest.
sessions.closingPrayer: Father, lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil. We're weaker than we pretend, and the danger is more real than we admit. Don't let the testing be more than we can bear, and rescue us from the evil we didn't invent and can't master alone. Keep us in the trials you allow, and deliver us from the darkness that would use them against us. And now, at the end, we hand back what was always yours: the kingdom we tried to keep, the power we thought was ours, the glory we kept taking. For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. We end this prayer smaller than we began it, and we've never been so safe. Amen.
reflection: Have I been praying as though I were stronger than I am, or asking not to be brought to the edge of my own weakness?
Where have I explained evil away, in the world or in myself, rather than asking to be delivered from it?
Which of the three, kingdom, power or glory, do I hold hardest, and what would it mean to hand it back?
sessions.teaching:
What should surprise us most about the Lord's Prayer is how it ends. We'd have ended it on a rising note, a declaration of victory. Jesus ends it with a request for rescue: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil" (Matthew 6:13). The last petition assumes two things we spend a lot of energy denying: that we're weaker than we think, and that the danger around us and inside us is more real than we admit. It's the prayer of someone who has stopped pretending.

First, the puzzle, because the church has struggled with this line and we shouldn't skip the struggle. James says as plainly as it can be said, "Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God,' for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one" (James 1:13). So why would Jesus teach us to ask God not to lead us into temptation, as though God were the tempter? Part of the answer is the Greek word, peirasmos, which means testing and trial as much as enticement to sin. Heard that way, the petition opens up. It isn't accusing God of luring us toward evil. It's a plea about the trials that come to every human life: don't let the testing be more than we can bear, don't leave us alone in the hour we couldn't survive. On the night he was arrested, Jesus told his sleepy disciples, "Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak" (Matthew 26:41).
