The petition is for people who know that about themselves. The puzzle is still alive today. In 2019 Pope Francis approved a new Italian wording of this line for the Mass, roughly "do not abandon us to temptation," to keep people from hearing God as the author of their temptation. God may test his children to strengthen them. He never entices them to evil. And this petition asks the God who permits the trial to be the God who delivers us through it.

Then the second half, "deliver us from evil," and here the modern objection deserves a fair hearing, because it's the reasonable voice in the room. The skeptic says evil is a primitive category, that what our ancestors called the evil one we now understand as psychology, trauma, poverty and circumstance, and that grown-ups don't pray to be rescued from a devil. A great deal of that is true. Evil has been used as a lazy explanation, a way to avoid examining our own hearts and our own systems. The church has cried "devil" at inconvenient people when the real problem was its own sin. A suspicion of superstition isn't faithlessness.

But look at the record of the age that makes the claim. Of all the centuries in which to announce that humanity had outgrown the category of evil, the twentieth was the strangest choice. It built the death camps, the gulags and the killing fields. It murdered by the million, with paperwork and efficiency and the participation of educated, cultured people. No account made only of psychology and circumstance has ever carried the whole weight of it. When Hannah Arendt watched Adolf Eichmann's trial in Jerusalem, she found the man shockingly ordinary and wrote of the banality of evil, and she still called it evil. Jesus didn't treat evil as a figure of speech. He told Peter, "Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail" (Luke 22:31-32). The petition doesn't require you to picture a cartoon devil. It requires only the honesty to admit there's a darkness in the world and in you that you didn't invent and can't master by yourself, and to ask, daily, to be delivered from it.

Then the prayer ends, and here we owe the group a plain fact. The oldest manuscripts of Matthew stop at "deliver us from evil," which is why most modern Bibles put the closing line in a footnote. But very early, in the Didache, a church manual from around the end of the first century, Christians were already closing the prayer with a shorter form, "for yours is the power and the glory forever." The fuller doxology echoes David's prayer: "Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty... Yours is the kingdom, O LORD" (1 Chronicles 29:11). For nearly two thousand years the people of God have ended this prayer the same way: "For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen."

See what that ending does. The prayer opened by hallowing God's name, and at every step since it has been making him larger and us smaller: his kingdom before our bread, his will before our wants, his mercy as the measure of ours, his deliverance because we can't save ourselves. Now it hands him three things by name, and they're exactly the three we spend our lives trying to keep. The kingdom is control. The power is strength. The glory is credit, the honor we keep quietly sending our own way. Most of us have tried to keep all three. I build small kingdoms and call them my life. I trust my own strength and hate to admit its limits. I take glory that was never mine in a hundred small thefts. The doxology is where all of it gets set down.

So we end this prayer smaller than we started it. We began by daring to call God Father, and we end by handing him the kingdom and the power and the glory and keeping nothing back. Every instinct says that's a loss. It isn't. The weight of the kingdom and the power and the glory was never ours to carry, and we were being crushed by property that wasn't ours. The safest place a human being has ever stood is here, at the end of this prayer, empty-handed before the God it belongs to, saying the last word the prayer gives us. Amen. So be it.

scriptureStudy.note: "And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil." The prayer ends in a plea for protection, admitting our weakness in the testing and our need of rescue from a real evil we can't overcome alone.

"Let no one say when he is tempted, 'I am being tempted by God,' for God cannot be tempted with evil, and he himself tempts no one." This governs how we read the petition. It pleads about the trial and never accuses God of authoring temptation.

"God is faithful, and he will not let you be tempted beyond your ability, but with the temptation he will also provide the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it." This is the promise beneath the petition.

"Watch and pray that you may not enter into temptation. The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak." In Gethsemane Jesus tells the disciples to pray the very petition he taught, tied to an admission of weakness.

"Simon, Simon, behold, Satan demanded to have you, that he might sift you like wheat, but I have prayed for you that your faith may not fail." Jesus names a real evil and answers it with prayer, the pattern the last petition puts in our mouths.

"Yours, O LORD, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty... Yours is the kingdom, O LORD." David's prayer is the likely root of the doxology the church added to the Lord's Prayer.
"To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!" The prayer's ending rehearses on earth what heaven sings forever.

sessions.goingDeeper:
For the group that wants to go further, look at the history of the ending. The doxology isn't in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew, and a careful group should hear that plainly rather than discover it later and feel misled. But the same history shows something moving. The Didache, a teaching manual from around the end of the first century or the start of the second, tells Christians to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day, and it closes the prayer with "for yours is the power and the glory forever." Within a generation or two of the apostles, the church was answering the darkness of the last petition with the sovereignty of God, in words drawn from David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29.

Then take up the secular witness on evil. Hannah Arendt's Eichmann in Jerusalem (1963) describes how ordinary and bureaucratic great evil can be, while refusing to reduce it to malfunction. She sees the symptom with great clarity; she doesn't offer a deliverance. Finally, notice how long the church has read this prayer as a summary of the Christian life: Tertullian around 200 called it a summary of the whole gospel; Augustine, writing to the widow Proba, said that whatever else we rightly pray is already contained in it; Luther, Calvin and the catechisms taught it line by line. Ask the group what it would look like to let this prayer shape all their other praying.
sessions.caseStudy:
Suppose a thoughtful skeptic has come to the group at a friend's invitation and has been patient through four sessions. The word evil is where he pushes back hardest. He says, without hostility, that he can appreciate much of this prayer as poetry and wisdom, but asking to be delivered from evil sounds like superstition, and he can't pretend to believe in a devil.

He isn't being difficult. He's being candid, and that's a gift to the room. Honor his intelligence rather than managing it. Don't rush to defend a cartoon devil, which isn't what the petition requires. Grant him what's true: evil has been used lazily and superstitiously, and his allergy to that is understandable. Then, without pressing him to believe anything, put a question back to him. Is the century just behind us best described by the word dysfunction, or does the word evil at some point become simply the accurate name for what happened?

Let him sit with it. The aim isn't to win tonight. It's to leave him unable to dismiss the category as naive, perhaps thinking he doesn't yet believe this prayer but no longer thinks believing it is stupid. Ask the group whether they've ever explained away evil in themselves the way the skeptic explains it away in the world.

memoryVerse.text: And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.

leaderPrimer:
The particular danger of a study on the Lord's Prayer is familiarity. Most people in your room have said these words since childhood, and familiarity doesn't deepen a thing; it numbs us to it. Everyone will arrive fairly sure they already know this prayer, and a room that already knows can't be taught. So the work of the first night is to make the familiar strange again, to slow the words down until people hear what they've been reciting for years. Don't let the group race ahead to the meaning. Stay in the actual words, one line a week, and trust that the prayer is deep enough to reward the slowness.

The second danger is that a study on prayer becomes a study about prayer, a set of ideas discussed and never a word actually prayed. Refuse that. Every session ends by praying the line it studied. If you do only one thing well, pray the prayer with your people rather than merely explaining it to them.

Take special care in two places. The forgiveness session, session 4, will land on someone carrying a deep wound, and this petition has been used as a whip on exactly such people. Don't press forgiveness on the wounded. Distinguish it clearly from excusing, from forgetting, and from going back within reach of someone still doing harm. Session 2 can touch the same nerve, because "your will be done" has been used to keep people in harm. Help information is printed with this guide, and Find Help on the site lists more; know where it is before the first night, and know a pastor or counselor you can refer someone to. And the final session names evil plainly, which a skeptic in the room may resist. Honor the resistance. The skeptic is often the most candid person present, and the goal isn't to win the argument but to leave him unable to call the faith stupid.

Lead from inside the prayer, not above it. If you present yourself as a master of prayer, the room will perform back at you and nothing will move. Go in as someone still learning to pray the prayer Jesus taught, still saying words your heart is catching up to. Five weeks won't make anyone a master of prayer. They can help a room hear, for the first time in years, the prayer they've been saying all their lives, and send people home able to pray it awake.

faq.q: Is this study just going to explain a prayer everyone already knows by heart?
faq.a: The fact that everyone knows it by heart is the problem the study is built to address. Familiarity numbs us, and many of us have said the Lord's Prayer so long we no longer hear it. The study slows the prayer down to one line a week so words worn smooth become sharp again: calling God Father, the cost of "your will be done," the candor of asking for bread, the hard word as in "forgive us as we forgive," and the humility of asking to be delivered from evil. The goal isn't to teach you a prayer you know but to help you pray the one you've been saying on autopilot.

faq.q: Do I need to know a lot about the Bible or theology to lead or join this study?
faq.a: No. A volunteer can lead it with little preparation, and anyone can join, including someone who has never prayed a serious prayer. Every discussion question carries notes for the leader, and every session ends by praying the line it studied. It takes up harder questions, like whether God tempts us, what daily bread means, and the condition in "forgive us as we forgive," but it handles them plainly and assumes no prior study. If you can read the prayer slowly and be candid about your own struggle to pray it, you can lead this.

faq.q: Why does the study spend so much time on the word as in "forgive us as we forgive"?
faq.a: Because it's the hardest word in the prayer and the one we most reliably skip. Jesus didn't say "forgive us because we forgive," as though we earned it. He said as, by the same measure, and then came back to it as soon as the prayer ended: "if you do not forgive others their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses" (Matthew 6:15). The study refuses both the reading that makes forgiveness a wage, which would wreck grace, and the reading that softens the word into nothing, which has to delete what Jesus said. Our forgiving doesn't buy God's. But someone who has received an ocean of mercy and withholds a cupful shows he never understood what he received.

faq.q: Session 4 talks about forgiveness. What if I've been deeply wounded and can't just forgive?
faq.a: The study takes this seriously and refuses the cruelty that has been done in this petition's name. Forgiveness has been used as a whip on the wounded, telling the betrayed and the abused that their healing depends on excusing what was done to them. That's a misuse the prayer never sponsored. Forgiveness isn't saying the wrong was fine. It isn't excusing or forgetting, and it is never going back within reach of someone still doing harm. It's the eventual release of your right to make the person pay, worked slowly by God for your own freedom, and it doesn't require reconciliation with someone unrepentant or dangerous. There's no timeline you owe anyone. If you're in danger, safety comes first; the help information printed with this guide says where to find it, and the leader will talk with you privately.

faq.q: Does the study say God might lead me into temptation? That sounds like blaming God for my sin.
faq.a: It faces that puzzle directly. James says God "tempts no one" (James 1:13), so whatever the petition means, it can't mean God is the author of our sin. The Greek word, peirasmos, means testing or trial as much as enticement, so the petition is best heard as a plea: don't let the testing be more than we can bear, don't leave us alone in it. God may test his children to strengthen them, but he never entices them to evil. In 2019 Pope Francis approved a new Italian wording of the line for the Mass, roughly "do not abandon us to temptation," to guard against the misreading.

faq.q: Is the ending, "for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory," actually in the Bible?
faq.a: It isn't in the earliest manuscripts of Matthew, which is why most modern Bibles put it in a footnote, and you deserve to know that. But it isn't a late invention either. The Didache, a church manual from around the end of the first century, already closes the prayer with a shorter form, "for yours is the power and the glory forever," and the fuller wording echoes David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11. The church was ending the prayer this way within a generation or two of the apostles, answering the darkness of the last petition with the sovereignty of God.

faq.q: I'm a skeptic. Isn't this just religion teaching people to recite words and feel spiritual?
faq.a: It's a fair suspicion, and Jesus shared part of it: he warned against heaping up "empty phrases" (Matthew 6:7). The study doesn't treat the prayer as a formula that works magic. It offers a slow reading of a prayer that, looked at closely, doesn't flatter the one who prays it. It puts God's name, kingdom and will before your needs. It asks you to surrender your will, depend for your bread, forgive as you'd be forgiven, and admit you're weaker than you think. You don't have to believe it to notice that it's stranger and more demanding than the religion you might have expected.

faq.q: How is this study structured, and how long does it take?
faq.a: Five sessions, one for each movement of the prayer. It can run as five weeks, as seven weeks with an opening and a closing night, or as a four-week intensive that pairs the first two sessions. Session 1 takes "Our Father in heaven, hallowed be your name." Session 2 takes "your kingdom come, your will be done." Session 3 takes daily bread. Session 4 takes "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." Session 5 takes "lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil," and the doxology. Each session runs about fifty minutes and closes by praying the line it studied. There's no homework, though a weekly practice is offered.

faq.q: What makes this different from other studies on the Lord's Prayer?
faq.a: Two things. It refuses to turn the prayer into a technique for getting what you want from God, because the prayer itself puts God first and is built to make us smaller and God larger. And it doesn't soften the hard parts. It stays with the word as, faces the puzzle about God and temptation, tells the plain truth about the doxology and the manuscripts, and names evil in a skeptical age. It writes toward the doubter and the wounded as much as the settled believer, giving the strongest objections their full weight before answering them.

faq.q: Can this study help someone who doesn't really know how to pray at all?
faq.a: That's who it was written for. The disciples who first heard this prayer didn't know how to pray either; that's why they asked, "Lord, teach us to pray" (Luke 11:1). Jesus didn't give them a technique or a mood. He gave them words, "Pray then like this" (Matthew 6:9), something to grow into. The study takes that seriously. It doesn't assume you arrive knowing how to pray, and it doesn't try to manufacture a feeling. It gives you the words Jesus gave, one line at a time, and lets them wait for your heart to catch up.

faq.q: Does taking this prayer seriously mean the study looks down on people whose minds wander when they pray?
faq.a: No. The study is candid that many of us pray the word Father for years before we can feel it, our minds on the calendar while our mouths say the words. A wandering mind isn't a disqualification; it's the ordinary condition of praying people. There's a gap that is hypocrisy and a gap that is faith reaching past the feeling, the way a wound heals before it feels healed. Jesus gave his friends words because they couldn't yet find their own. The point is never to make anyone feel they pray badly, but to help everyone, the struggler most of all, hear the prayer they've been saying.

timeline.event: Jesus teaches the prayer, in Matthew within the Sermon on the Mount and in Luke in answer to the request, "Lord, teach us to pray."
In Gethsemane Jesus prays "Abba, Father" and "not my will, but yours, be done," showing that surrender is trust that passes through real desire, not resignation.
Paul writes to the Galatians and the Romans that the Spirit of adoption puts the word Jesus used, "Abba! Father!", in the mouths of believers.

timeline.date: late first or early second century
timeline.event: The Didache, an early Christian teaching manual, tells believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day and closes it with a short doxology, "for yours is the power and the glory forever."
Tertullian writes On Prayer, calling the Lord's Prayer a summary of the whole gospel.
Cyprian of Carthage writes On the Lord's Prayer, dwelling on the boldness of calling God Father and on the plural petitions: the Christian never prays for himself alone.
Origen writes On Prayer, noting that he can find the word translated daily, epiousios, in no other Greek writer and thinks the Gospel writers coined it.
Augustine writes to the widow Proba about prayer (Letter 130), teaching that whatever else we rightly pray is already contained in the petitions of the Lord's Prayer.
Martin Luther writes A Simple Way to Pray for his barber, Peter, teaching him to pray by walking slowly through the Lord's Prayer petition by petition.
John Calvin, in the final edition of his Institutes (book 3, chapter 20), expounds the Lord's Prayer line by line and answers the objection that prayer is pointless if God is sovereign.
The Westminster Shorter Catechism expounds the Lord's Prayer petition by petition, as the Heidelberg Catechism had done in 1563.
Pope Francis approves a new Italian wording of the Lord's Prayer for the Mass, "do not abandon us to temptation," to guard against hearing God as the author of temptation.

facilitatorScript.open: Welcome, and thank you for being here. We're going to do something a little strange with a prayer most of us have known since we were children: we're going to slow it down and actually hear it. Before we start, three things. First, familiarity is the thing to watch for tonight. The goal isn't to prove we already know this prayer but to hear it as if for the first time, and there are no wrong answers in the first few minutes. Second, we aren't here to perform. You can say your mind wanders when you pray, or that you've said these words for years without meaning them. That's exactly where we start, and what's said here stays here. Third, I'm not up here as someone who has mastered this prayer. I'm still learning to pray it, like all of us. One more thing. If this study touches a real wound, especially in the session on forgiveness, you don't have to resolve it on anyone's schedule. I'm available to talk privately, and there's help information printed with this guide. Tonight we're sitting with this line: ________. I'll read our key passage, and then we'll sit with it before anyone says anything.
facilitatorScript.transition: We've looked hard at what this line says. Now let's bring it off the page and into the prayers each of us actually prays, or doesn't, because none of this matters if it stays an idea about prayer in general instead of the prayer you'll try to say this week.
facilitatorScript.close: We're going to stop there, even though it doesn't tie up neatly. A prayer isn't a problem solved in an evening. Take this line home with you. Try the practice this week, even badly, and sit with the reflection questions on your own. And before we go, we're going to do the one thing this whole study is finally about. We're going to pray the line we just studied, together and slowly, and mean it as best we can. Thank you for coming, and my door is open if any of you needs it.

cadences.name: The full study (7 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Orientation. Read the summary together, name familiarity as the thing to watch for, and pray the whole prayer through slowly once, hearing it before studying it.
Week 2: Session 1, Our Father in Heaven, Hallowed Be Your Name, the address and the reverence held together.
Week 3: Session 2, Your Kingdom Come, Your Will Be Done, with extended time on Gethsemane and praying against our own preferences.
Week 4: Session 3, Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread, dependence, the manna, and the freedom of enough.
Week 5: Session 4, Forgive Us Our Debts, As We Forgive, with careful time on the word as, private space for the wounded, and the help information at hand.
Week 6: Session 5, Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil, the final petition and the doxology.
Week 7: Integration. Pray the whole prayer through together line by line, revisit the practices, and close on the kingdom, the power, and the glory handed back to God.

cadences.name: The intensive (4 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Sessions 1 and 2 together, the address and reverence, then the kingdom and the will.
Week 2: Session 3, Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread, dependence and enough.
Week 3: Session 4, Forgive Us Our Debts, As We Forgive, with care for the wounded in the room and the help information at hand.
Week 4: Session 5, Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil, plus a short integration close praying the whole prayer through.

cadences.name: As written (5 weeks)
plan: Week 1: Session 1, Our Father in Heaven, Hallowed Be Your Name.
Week 2: Session 2, Your Kingdom Come, Your Will Be Done.
Week 3: Session 3, Give Us This Day Our Daily Bread.
Week 4: Session 4, Forgive Us Our Debts, As We Forgive.
Week 5: Session 5, Lead Us Not Into Temptation, But Deliver Us From Evil.

bibliography.title: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God
bibliography.author: Timothy Keller
bibliography.note: Keller (2014) holds together the awe and the closeness that session 1 insists on, and treats the Lord's Prayer as a school of Christian prayer. Background for sessions 1 and 5.

bibliography.title: The Lord and His Prayer
bibliography.author: N. T. Wright
bibliography.note: Wright (1996) walks through the prayer petition by petition, reading it within the story of Jesus and the kingdom. Background for every session, especially session 2.

bibliography.title: Letters to Malcolm: Chiefly on Prayer
bibliography.author: C. S. Lewis
bibliography.note: Lewis's informal letters on prayer (1964), candid about the wandering mind and the strangeness of asking. Background for sessions 1 and 3; not quoted.

bibliography.title: On the Lord's Prayer
bibliography.author: Cyprian of Carthage
bibliography.note: The third-century treatise (about 252) on the boldness of calling God Father and on the plural of the petitions. Background for sessions 1 and 3.

bibliography.title: On Prayer
bibliography.author: Origen of Alexandria
bibliography.note: The treatise (about 233) that notes the rare word epiousios and reflects on the whole prayer. Background for session 3.

bibliography.title: A Simple Way to Pray
bibliography.author: Martin Luther
bibliography.note: Luther's letter to his barber (1535), teaching prayer by walking slowly through the Lord's Prayer. A model for the study's method.

bibliography.title: Institutes of the Christian Religion, Book 3, Chapter 20
bibliography.author: John Calvin
bibliography.note: Calvin's fullest treatment of prayer, expounding the Lord's Prayer and answering the objection that prayer is pointless under God's sovereignty. Background for session 2.

bibliography.title: Waiting for God
bibliography.author: Simone Weil
bibliography.note: Includes Weil's meditation on the Our Father. A demanding and unconventional voice, offered as a witness rather than a settled guide. Background for sessions 2 and 5.

bibliography.title: Eichmann in Jerusalem: A Report on the Banality of Evil
bibliography.author: Hannah Arendt
bibliography.note: Arendt's report on the 1961 Eichmann trial (1963), naming how ordinary great evil can be while refusing to reduce it to malfunction. Cited in session 5.

bibliography.title: The Prayers of Jesus
bibliography.author: Joachim Jeremias
bibliography.note: Jeremias's study (English translation 1967) arguing for the closeness of the word Abba. Cited in session 1; read it alongside Barr's correction.

bibliography.title: "Abba Isn't 'Daddy'" (Journal of Theological Studies, 1988)
bibliography.author: James Barr
bibliography.note: Barr's essay correcting the popular claim that Abba simply means Daddy. Cited in session 1 to keep the closeness of the address real without making it childish.

bibliography.title: The Gospel of Matthew
bibliography.author: Matthew
bibliography.note: The primary text: chapter 6, where the prayer is given within the Sermon on the Mount. Read it and pray it, not only cite it.

furtherReading: Prayer: Experiencing Awe and Intimacy with God, Timothy Keller, for those who want a fuller pastoral account of holding awe and closeness together.
The Lord and His Prayer, N. T. Wright, for a short walk through the prayer within the story of the kingdom.
A Simple Way to Pray, Martin Luther, for anyone who wants to practice praying the prayer slowly, line by line.
Institutes, book 3, chapter 20, John Calvin, for those willing to sit with session 2's question of how prayer and God's sovereignty hold together.
The Gospel of Matthew, chapters 5 to 7, read straight through, to hear the prayer in the setting Jesus gave it.

glossary.definition: The Aramaic word for father that Jesus used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36), a word of family closeness. Real and deep without being a nursery word, as the debate between Jeremias and James Barr made clear, and now placed in the believer's mouth by the Spirit (Romans 8:15).
Treated as holy, set apart. To pray "hallowed be your name" is to ask that God's name be known and honored as holy, which lines us up with God's own purpose before we ask anything for ourselves.

God's reign breaking into the world, prayed for in the present tense. Not acceptance of the way things are but their overturning, feeding the hungry and bringing down the mighty (Luke 1:52-53), which is why praying for it makes a person restless for justice.
The daily surrender of our own way to God's, as Jesus prayed in Gethsemane, where he named what he wanted and then laid it down. Surrender in trust, not resignation in defeat.

The rare Greek word translated daily in "give us this day our daily bread." Origen could find it in no other Greek writer. Its exact sense is debated, but it points to bread for the day rather than for the storehouse.

The ordinary provision the prayer asks for, one day at a time. It admits that we didn't make ourselves and can't keep ourselves, and because it says "give us," it draws the one praying into feeding the hungry.
The small word in "forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors." We don't earn forgiveness by forgiving, but refusing to forgive shows we haven't understood the mercy we received.

The Greek word in "lead us not into temptation," meaning testing or trial as much as enticement to evil. Read this way, the petition asks not to be left alone in the trial and never accuses God, who tempts no one (James 1:13).

The plea for rescue that ends the prayer itself, admitting a real evil in the world and in us that we didn't invent and can't master alone. It requires no cartoon devil, only the candor the last century made hard to avoid.

The closing line, "for yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever." Absent from the earliest manuscripts of Matthew, present in a shorter form in the Didache, and echoing David's prayer in 1 Chronicles 29:11.
The distinction at the heart of "your will be done." Resignation is giving up because nothing can be done. Surrender is laying down what you wanted into hands you believe are good.
The prayer's order: God's name, kingdom and will before our bread. The whole prayer makes the one praying smaller and God larger, the opposite of prayer as a technique for getting what we want.
An early Christian teaching manual from the late first or early second century. It tells believers to pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day and closes it with a short doxology.

promoKit.bulletinBlurb: Almost everyone knows the Lord's Prayer by heart, and almost no one hears it anymore. This five-session study slows the prayer Jesus taught down to one line a week, until words worn smooth by repetition become sharp again: calling God Father, the cost of "your will be done," asking for daily bread, the hard word as in "forgive us as we forgive," and asking to be delivered from evil. It takes up the hard questions plainly, including whether God tempts us and whether the doxology is in the Bible, and it ends where the prayer ends, handing God the kingdom, the power and the glory. Anyone can lead it with little preparation. Come and hear the prayer you've been saying all your life.
promoKit.pulpitAnnouncement: We're starting a five-week study on the Lord's Prayer, and if you think you already know it, that's exactly the problem. Most of us have said these words since childhood and stopped hearing them years ago. This study slows the prayer down to one line a week and helps us pray it awake again. It handles the hard parts plainly: the puzzle about God and temptation, what "forgive us as we forgive" asks of us, and the truth about the doxology. It's written for the doubter and the wounded as much as the settled believer. No homework, and no preparation needed to lead a group. Every session ends by praying the line it studied. Sign up at the welcome table.
promoKit.inviteCaption: You know the Lord's Prayer by heart. When did you last hear it? A five-session study on the prayer Jesus taught, one line a week, past the recitation and into the words: Abba, your will be done, daily bread, forgive us as we forgive, and the kingdom and the power and the glory handed back to God. Come and hear it.
quoteCards: You can recite the Lord's Prayer for years and never once hear its first word. Father.
"Your will be done" isn't where desire dies. It's where desire finds something good enough to hold it.
We ask for more because we think enough will finally make us safe. It never has.
The hardest word in the prayer is the small one we never notice. As.
The forgiven forgive, not to earn what they were given but because they have it.
The century that thought it had outgrown the word evil built the death camps.
The prayer hands God back the three things we spend our lives trying to keep: the kingdom, the power and the glory.
We end this prayer smaller than we began it, and we've never been so safe.
